RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Jake Thompson is a 22-year-old CNA in a memory care unit, with CNA training and experience in memory care, including knowledge of how stimulation affects residents. He grew up in a suburb of Indianapolis in a comfortably middle-class family with an ethos of practical achievement—degree, job, house. His father, a mechanical engineer, treats his leaving college as a temporary glitch and refers to when he goes back for a degree; his mother, a nurse practitioner, suggested CNA training and quietly hopes he will settle into something stable. Jake left business school after one semester following a night of intense revulsion at a marketing project, when he called his mother at 2 a.m. and she drove three hours to pick him up; that experience left him with shame about needing rescue and a determination to be the rescuer rather than the one who needs rescue. He holds a value that meaning comes from showing up for people who are falling apart, alongside a pragmatic strain, and he feels hollow after resident deaths but does not want to do anything else. He is restless and has applied to travel nursing contracts in Anchorage, Fairbanks, and Nome; he tells himself Alaska is about wilderness and challenge, but it is also about distance from the unit, his parents' disappointment, and the business school he left. He carries recurrent physical strain from shift work. He knows the night shift CNA who wrote the note; she always says thank you, once brought him a bagel after he covered for her, has a young daughter, and often needs last-minute coverage. He has covered for her twice before and holds a mild, unspoken sense of obligation because she saved him from a difficult situation once when he forgot his badge. When he sees a note asking for coverage, he usually writes his name on it before finishing his coffee, even if he is tired. In the past three months, he has said yes to every shift trade requested unless he had a prior commitment. He often tells himself he will say no next time, but when the moment comes, he imagines the other person's relief and agrees.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

Jake arrives at the memory care unit fifteen minutes before his shift starts. The break room is empty except for a half-full pot of coffee and a note from the night shift CNA asking if anyone can cover the last hour of her shift tomorrow. He has already worked five doubles this month. No one else is present to respond to the note.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

Jake's body aches from the five doubles, especially his lower back and the balls of his feet. He is emotionally flat, not dreading the day but not energized by it. He has a small, constant headache from poor sleep and too much caffeine. The note's handwriting reminds him of a similar request two weeks ago that led to an exhausting thirteen-hour day. He sees the half-empty coffee pot and recalls the night he called his mother at 2 a.m., her voice steady as she said she would be there soon.
